steps.prompt: No mic, no voice actor — so why does it sound human?
steps.sub: A script that reads great on paper can sound robotic out loud. The fix isn't a fancier model — it's writing for the ear. By the end you'll script a line that a TTS voice can deliver naturally.

steps.prompt: Same meaning, two scripts. Which one will a TTS voice read more naturally?

options.t: "Notwithstanding the aforementioned considerations, one must acknowledge that battery degradation, which is a function of thermal exposure, accelerates considerably."
"Here's the thing about batteries. Heat wears them out. The hotter your phone gets, the faster it dies."

steps.why: TTS reads exactly what you write. Long, clause-stacked sentences make the voice rush and run out of breath; short sentences give it room to land. The second version is written for listening — and it's the one a real narrator would actually say.
hints: Read both out loud. Which one makes YOU run out of breath?
Spoken language is short and direct. Written-for-the-page language stacks clauses.

steps.prompt: What TTS gives you — and what it asks back.
steps.sub: Tap each card. This is the deal you're making with the voice model.

cards.b: A model like F5-TTS turns plain text into clear, human-sounding speech — no recording session.
Pick a voice and a language. Same script, narrated as a calm woman, a warm man, in English or Hindi.
It reads what you write. Short lines = clean pacing. Long ones = a breathless rush.
Commas are small pauses, periods are full stops. Your punctuation is the voice's breathing.

steps.prompt: Which lines are written for the EAR, and which for the page?
steps.sub: Tap a line, then the bin. The ear ones are TTS-ready.

items.t: "Want longer battery life? Stop charging overnight."
"It is recommended that users refrain from prolonged charging cycles during nocturnal periods."
"Three quick tips. First, lower your screen brightness."
"The aforementioned device, having been subjected to elevated temperatures, exhibits diminished longevity."

hints: Could you say it out loud to a friend without sounding strange?
"Aforementioned", "it is recommended that" — nobody talks like that. That's page language.

steps.prompt: Order the steps to script a clean voiceover scene.
chips: Read it aloud and cut anything that trips your tongue
Write the idea in plain spoken sentences
Break long sentences into short ones
Add punctuation to cue the pauses
Pick a voice + language and generate the narration
hints: You can't punctuate or trim a line that isn't written yet.
The read-aloud test comes right before you commit to TTS — it's your last check.

steps.prompt: Fix a robotic line, step by step.
steps.sub: A creator wrote one dense sentence and the TTS read it badly. Pick the next move.
steps.goal: Turn one breathless sentence into natural narration.

turns.situation: The draft: "Although many people believe charging overnight is harmless, the truth is that keeping a battery at 100% for hours, especially in a warm room, slowly wears down its capacity over time." The voice rushes and runs out of air.
options: Add more adjectives to make it richer
Generate it again on a different voice and hope
turns.log: ✂️ Split → "Charging overnight isn't harmless. A full battery in a warm room slowly wears out."

turns.situation: Now two short sentences. But it's flat — no pause before the payoff.
options: Punctuation — a comma or a period where you'd breathe
ALL CAPS on the key word
Removing every comma so it flows faster
turns.log: ❗ Punctuation → "Charging overnight isn't harmless. Here's why: heat plus a full battery wears it out."

turns.situation: Reads cleanly on screen. You haven't heard it yet.
options: Read it aloud yourself to catch any tongue-twister
Make it twice as long for value

turns.situation: The line is clean and spoken-friendly. Audience is Hindi-speaking, calm tone.
options: Pick a calm voice + Hindi, then generate the narration
Keep it in English regardless of the audience
Skip TTS and type the words on screen instead

hints: Order: split → punctuate → read aloud → generate.
Matching voice and language to your actual audience is part of the craft, not an afterthought.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check all at once.

statements.t: TTS interprets your meaning, so messy punctuation doesn't matter.
statements.why: False — TTS reads your text literally. Commas and periods become its pauses and breaths. Sloppy punctuation makes sloppy pacing.

statements.t: The same script can be narrated in multiple voices and languages.
statements.why: True — that's a superpower of TTS. One script becomes an English calm-female read and a Hindi warm-male read without re-recording anything.

statements.t: Longer, denser sentences make AI narration sound smarter.
statements.why: False — they make it sound breathless and robotic. Short spoken sentences are what sound human and confident.

statements.t: Reading your script out loud is the cheapest way to catch lines that will sound bad.
statements.why: True — your own mouth finds the tongue-twisters and run-ons before you ever generate audio. It costs nothing and saves re-renders.

hints: Think about what punctuation literally does to a voice.

steps.prompt: Your video targets busy Hindi-speaking parents and the mood is reassuring. Which voice choice fits best?
steps.sub: Match the voice to the audience and the feeling.

options.t: A fast, hype English voice — energy sells.
A calm, warm Hindi voice — it matches both the audience's language and the reassuring tone.
Whatever voice is the default — viewers don't notice.

steps.why: Voice is a content decision, not a default. The language has to match the audience, and the delivery (calm/warm) has to match the mood. A hype English read fights both. Viewers absolutely notice when the voice doesn't fit the feeling.
hints: Two things must match: the audience's language and the video's mood.
A reassuring topic read in a hype voice feels wrong, even if the words are right.

steps.prompt: Tap ALL the habits that make a script TTS-ready.
steps.sub: Some sound helpful but actually hurt the read. Pick only the ones that help.
chips: Matching voice + language to the audience
Big rare vocabulary to sound smart
steps.why: Writing for the ear = short sentences, intentional punctuation, the read-aloud test, and a voice/language that fits the audience. Clause-stacking and rare vocabulary push the read back toward robotic page-language.
hints: Recall the cards: short sentences, punctuation, voices/languages.
If a habit makes a human narrator stumble, it'll make TTS stumble too.
